newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan sushi chain is latest 'bubble' debt casualty.
newsitem.headline: Japan sushi chain is latest 'bubble' debt casualty.

text.p: A chain of sushi restaurants said on Monday it had sought protection from creditors under Japan's bankruptcy laws, becoming the latest corporate casualty of the nation's "bubble" era excesses.
The company, Kyotaru Co Ltd, said it made the insolvency filing on Sunday at a Tokyo court with huge debts totalling some $865 million.
Kyotaru is the first firm listed on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange to fail since mid-1993.
Kyotaru buckled under the weight of debts resulting from rapid domestic expansion and investment in the United States during Japan's 1980s bubble of soaring asset prices and unbridled consumption.
The firm, which offers take-out sushi as well as running sushi restaurants, was also hard hit by a food poisoning epidemic that swept Japan last year and made customers wary of eating uncooked food.

Under the filing at Tokyo District Court, Kyotaru will seek to restructure and salvage parts of its business under court protection. The company said its debts totalled 101.3 billion yen ($865 million), far exceeding its assets, worth 62.26 billion yen ($532 million).

It is the first firm from the bourse's first section -- the main section for big-name companies -- to fail since July 1993, when Nikkatsu Corp, a movie company, went bust with debts of about 50 billion yen ($427 million).

The legacy of debt and bad loans left by the collapse of the economic bubble in the early 1990s is still pushing many troubled companies to the wall, even though the economy as a whole has shown signs of stirring back to life.
The recent big business failures include loan firms Nichiei Finance and All Corp as well as realtor Sueno Kosan and major Japanese jeweller Coco Yamaoka Hoshokuten.

Kyotaru, established in 1950 and employing just over 1,800 people, plans to strive for "business as usual" while streamlining operations at inefficient restaurants and divisions, Japanese newspapers reported.

Under Japan's Corporate Rehabilitation Law, the assets of a financially strapped company are protected from creditors by the court if the court decides to proceed with the company's request for restructuring.

Kyotaru shares were placed under surveillance on Monday -- a formal procedure in which dealing authorities signal caution about particular shares -- before being delisted from the exchange on April 20. ($1=117 yen)
